html:
The map's "Seljuk Caliphate" is the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, a Turkish state in central Anatolia ruled from Konya. "Rum" means Rome: the land had been Byzantine. The Seljuks were sultans, never caliphs.

It began after the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071, when Turkish groups moved into Anatolia. A branch of the Seljuk family built a state there and beat the Byzantines again at Myriokephalon in 1176. In the early 1200s it was at its height: caravanserais lined its trade roads, and Persian was the language of its court. The poet Rumi lived and taught in Konya.

In 1243 the Mongols crushed the Seljuk army at Köse Dağ. After that the sultans were puppets of the Ilkhanate, and the line ended around 1308. By the later dates the map shows, central Anatolia was in fact divided among the Turkish beyliks, such as Karaman, while one of them, the Ottomans, grew in the north-west.
